title: Run typecheck, lint and tests in CI
description:
CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs only the backlog checks today. The product checks — npm run
typecheck, npm run lint, npm run test — are missing from it.

Found during the shady2k-skills setup; filed with it. Adopted by lifemodel-ggc (self-change-1 outcome 3), stage lifemodel-ggc.1.

## Change (short spec delta, owner-approved preflight 2026-10-08)
1. package.json gets `check`: typecheck, lint, format:check, then `vitest run --maxWorkers=2`, stopping at the first failure with its exit code. AGENTS.md's Commands table lists it.
2. The two files on main that fail `npm run format:check` (domain-trackers.ts, status-update-service.ts) are formatted (a repair the merge waits on).
3. A classifier script under scripts/ reads changed paths (one per line) and answers whether product checks are owed. Not product: `.beads/**`, `docs/**`, `*.md` at the repository root, `.backlog/**`, `.githooks/*`, `scripts/connect-clone.sh`. Everything else is product (including .github/, package*.json, src/**/*.md, the classifier itself). An empty list is product (an empty diff is no evidence of safety).
4. ci.yml: a `changes` job runs the classifier on the PR's merge-base...head diff, or on a push's before..after diff (a missing or all-zero `before` means product). A `ci-product` job needs it, runs only when product is owed and the PR is not a draft: checkout, setup-node 24 with npm cache, `npm ci`, `npm run check`. `ci-backlog` is unchanged.
5. AGENTS.md and docs/backlog-integration.md (Full stage checks, CI, the hooks paragraph that says CI will be the product checks' home) describe the result; the ci.yml header comment too.

## Scenarios
- `npm run check` on a clean tree exits 0; a planted type error, lint error, formatting slip or failing test each makes it exit non-zero.
- classifier: [docs/x.md] -> no; [README.md] -> no; [.beads/issues.jsonl, AGENTS.md] -> no; [src/a.ts] -> yes; [docs/x.md, package.json] -> yes; [src/runtime/builtin-skills/s/SKILL.md] -> yes; [.github/workflows/ci.yml] -> yes; [] -> yes.

DONE WHEN: a CI job runs typecheck, lint and the vitest suite on pull requests and pushes to main,
with node 24 and npm ci; a change that cannot touch product code does not owe them.

title: A person starts their own lifemodel instance from the Docker image with one command
description:
Charter: docs/charters/instance-1.md, outcome 4 (re-cut 2026-10-08). Design decisions (1)-(16) with their evidence are in this issue's comments; this body is the spec.

## Problem
Today lifemodel runs only from a developer's checkout: `npm run dev` with an `.env`, Node and native libraries installed by hand, keys in plain environment variables the agent's own process can read, nothing that stops it or brings it back when it breaks. A person who wants their own lifemodel cannot start one, and an agent that rewrites its own code holds every key and can disable anything meant to stop it.

## Solution
A person runs one `docker run` command with the published image. They open `boot.localhost` (through an SSH tunnel on a VPS), set the loader's password, and the loader brings up lifemodel. They put the model key into Agent Vault (`vault.localhost`, reached through the loader's login), open lifemodel's own interface at the root host and set the endpoint and the models. lifemodel then talks to the model with the key injected on the way out, never holding it. The owner can panic the instance from the loader or the command line, and it stays down through restarts until resumed. Recreating the container keeps lifemodel's code and data.

## Stories
- S1 First start. As a person with Docker, I run the documented command on an empty volume; the loader starts, `boot.localhost` asks me to set a password, and after I set it the loader creates the instance's git repository on the volume from the code the image carries, builds it, and starts lifemodel. Nothing asks me for a key at this point.
- S2 Login. Every page of `boot.`, the root host and `vault.` requires the loader's login; one login (a cookie on the parent domain) opens all three; a wrong password is refused and logged at warn without the password.
- S3 Keys. As the owner I add the model key to Agent Vault through `vault.` (its own interface) and a service for my endpoint's host with bearer auth. lifemodel's settings show only a placeholder and a link to the loader for keys. The key never appears in lifemodel's process environment, its config, its logs or its data.
- S4 lifemodel's settings. In lifemodel's own interface at the root host I set the OpenAI-compatible endpoint (base URL), the model for each role (fast, smart, motor), and the Telegram fields (chat id; the bot token as an Agent Vault placeholder). Saving applies them: lifemodel restarts through the loader with the new settings. These settings belong to lifemodel's code, which may extend them later.
- S5 A model request. lifemodel's request to the endpoint leaves through Agent Vault; the endpoint receives `Authorization: Bearer <the key from Agent Vault>`. A direct connection from lifemodel's user that bypasses the proxy is refused by the kernel rule, and that refusal is visible in lifemodel's log as a connection error, not a silent hang.
- S6 Panic. `docker exec <c> lifemodel panic` or the loader's button stops lifemodel (its turn drained as on any stop) and marks panic in a place lifemodel's user cannot write. While panic is set, the loader stays up but does not start lifemodel - after `docker restart` and after a restart of the Docker daemon alike. `lifemodel resume` (or the button) clears it and starts lifemodel. `lifemodel status` says whether lifemodel runs, on which commit, and whether panic is set.
- S7 Recreate. `docker rm -f` and the same `docker run` on the same volume bring back the same instance: the same repository and commit, the same data, the same loader password and Agent Vault contents; the image's code does not overwrite the instance's repository.
- S8 Stop. `docker stop` gives lifemodel its drain (the restart guarantee of outcome 2) before the container ends; the documented command sets a stop timeout long enough for it.
- S9 Image. Every pull request that touches product code builds the image in CI as a check; every push to main publishes it to `ghcr.io/shady2k/lifemodel` (tags `main` and the commit).

## Decisions
- The image holds the runtime (Node 24, native libraries for onnx, sharp, LanceDB, git) and a TRUSTED LAYER lifemodel cannot see or change: the LOADER, CADDY and AGENT VAULT, run as root-owned processes; lifemodel runs as an unprivileged user. The loader starts first and owns the others; it is the container's main process.
- Volume layout (one volume): the instance's git repository (lifemodel's code; seeded once from the code the image carries, with upstream as a remote; never overwritten by a newer image), the build of the current commit, lifemodel's data (state, logs, config, models), and root-only directories for the loader (password hash, panic flag, its own state) and Agent Vault (its store, passwordless mode: protection is the directory's permissions).
- Only what lifemodel must not change sits in the loader: its login, panic, first start. Model endpoint, models, Telegram and every other setting are lifemodel's own (decision 9). Generations, self-healing and maintenance are outcome 5.
- The loader's web interface is always on, independent of lifemodel. Its command line inside the container is `lifemodel status|panic|resume`.
- Front door: Caddy is the only web entrance. Routing by host: the root host is lifemodel's interface, `boot.` the loader, `vault.` Agent Vault (its interface uses absolute paths, so it cannot sit under a subpath). Caddy asks the loader to check every request (forward_auth); one cookie on the parent domain. Listens on localhost only in this outcome; built so a domain and certificates can be added later (idea lifemodel-sd2).
- lifemodel's egress: an iptables owner rule lets lifemodel's user connect only to Agent Vault's proxy port (and loopback services it needs); the rule is installed by the loader as root before lifemodel starts; the container needs NET_ADMIN, and nothing else beyond defaults. lifemodel's vault in Agent Vault is NOT strict: known services get their key, other hosts pass through (lifemodel reads news and the web); strict deny is for tasks (outcome 6). lifemodel's process uses the proxy through the standard proxy environment and trusts Agent Vault's CA.
- Keys: the model key by bearer auth on the endpoint's host; the Telegram token by placeholder substitution in the request path (Agent Vault supports path, query, header and body substitution). lifemodel's config holds placeholders only.
- lifemodel's model configuration becomes one OpenAI-compatible endpoint (base URL) with a model per role; no key in lifemodel. The existing provider code is extended, not duplicated (one surface per capability); OpenRouter remains reachable as just another OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
- Agent Vault's version is pinned in the image and updated deliberately (its API is still changing).
- Embeddings stay local (downloaded to the volume on first use).
- Failures explain themselves: the loader logs to stdout (the container log) with a component name; a refused login, a failed first build, a refused start under panic and a stop that ran past the drain are each one line saying what and why; secrets never appear in any log.

## Checks
The seams, all reached from outside the container the way a person does:
- C1 the documented `docker run` command and `docker exec <c> lifemodel status|panic|resume` (exit codes and output);
- C2 HTTP against Caddy with `Host:` headers `boot.localhost`, `localhost`, `vault.localhost` (login refused/accepted, pages reachable only with the cookie);
- C3 a STUB OpenAI-compatible endpoint in the test environment that answers a fixed completion and records the headers it receives: proves the key arrives injected;
- C4 lifemodel's process environment, config file and logs inside the container contain no key (checked by reading them);
- C5 a direct connection from lifemodel's user to an outside address is refused;
- C6 `docker restart`, a restart of the Docker daemon, `docker rm -f` + `docker run` on the same volume;
- C7 the CI workflow: the image builds on a pull request with product changes and is published on main.
Unit tests through the loader's own interfaces (first start, panic flag, login) with doubles only at the process and filesystem boundaries; the end-to-end walk above is the acceptance. The model key used is a made-up string; no real Telegram or keys.

## Out
- Generations, self-healing, maintenance mode, migrations (outcome 5).
- The task executor and Motor Cortex without Docker (outcome 6); in the image Motor Cortex answers that Docker is unavailable, as it already does.
- Access from outside: own domain, certificates, Let's Encrypt (idea lifemodel-sd2).
- Remote embeddings; custom request headers (lifemodel adds them later itself).
- Spend limits (lifemodel-ld6).
- Updates from upstream into an existing instance (upstream-1).

## DONE WHEN
On a clean test machine with Docker, one command starts the image from CI; the owner sets the loader's password, puts the model key into Agent Vault through the loader, sets the endpoint and models in lifemodel's own interface; lifemodel's model request reaches the endpoint with the key injected by Agent Vault while no key is in lifemodel's process; recreating the container keeps the code and the data; panic keeps it down across a restart of the container and of Docker until it is resumed. Where it is seen: the browser at boot.localhost / localhost / vault.localhost (through an SSH tunnel on a VPS), `docker exec <c> lifemodel status`, and the stub endpoint's recorded request.

comments.text:
Owner decisions 2026-10-08 (design discussion for instance-1 outcomes 4-6; research by two background reads, key claims checked):
(1) Motor Cortex becomes a TASK EXECUTOR: several tasks at once, one prime-agent per task, each with its own profile (files, network, resources, time); self-change is one kind of task, others work on other repositories. prime-agent is lifemodel's hands: a self-change task has full access to the instance's code and data. lifemodel picks a task's profile, the owner sets the ceilings; a trusted executor baked into the image (root, beside the supervisor) launches and confines each task and refuses a request above the ceilings.
(2) Isolation inside the one container (only Docker on the host): per-task uid + Landlock (files) + an iptables owner rule sending the task's traffic only to the egress proxy + rlimits. Evidence: in a default Docker container user/net namespaces are blocked (unshare -U: Operation not permitted, tested here), so srt/Codex sandbox/bubblewrap/nsjail/firejail/gVisor do not fit; Landlock ABI 7 works (tested); /sys/fs/cgroup is read-only (no per-task cgroups; container-wide --memory/--cpus is the outer cap). Needs one container capability: NET_ADMIN. Ready-made per-task platforms either need KVM (microsandbox, E2B, Docker Sandboxes, Kata, Firecracker) or host-root via the Docker socket / privileged DinD (Daytona OSS, container-use, OpenHands) - rejected.
(3) The executor's interface is shaped so microsandbox (microVM per task, host-side domain policy, TS SDK, only --device /dev/kvm) can be added later as a second backend where KVM exists.
(4) Secrets never enter task processes (and, where feasible, not lifemodel itself): all task egress goes through Infisical Agent Vault (github.com/Infisical/agent-vault, MIT core) in strict-deny mode - it is the domain allowlist and injects credentials from placeholders; per-task role = allowed services + credentials. Its management port is unreachable to tasks (iptables allows only the proxy port); tasks trust its MITM CA (NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS). OpenBao dropped: Agent Vault's own encrypted store suffices; Infisical as a source later for short-lived secrets. Owner uses Agent Vault in his homelab.

comments.author: claude-coordinator:shady2k@vm-agents:main#e5607568
comments.text:
Owner decisions 2026-10-08, continued:
(5) Name: the trusted component is the LOADER (the project's word from ADR-006: a trusted loader runs numbered generations, boot-state, A/B slots for its own update); 'supervisor' is not used. The loader is also the BOOTSTRAP: an empty volume opens the setup wizard (model endpoint and key, models, Telegram, embeddings local or remote); every later start boots the selected generation. One entry point for install, normal boot and maintenance.
(6) Maintenance mode 'like BIOS/UEFI': the loader lists generations and the owner picks one to boot; entered by hand (a start flag or docker exec) or automatically after N consecutive generations fail to come up. Self-healing: a new generation that does not come up healthy is replaced by the previous healthy one, with a report.
(7) The loader has its OWN WEB INTERFACE (not Telegram) for the setup wizard, the generation list and panic: by default it listens on localhost only (access through an SSH tunnel); the owner may open it outside behind his own HTTPS proxy.
(8) DATA IS NEVER ROLLED BACK - a generation is code only; Telegram history and external memory cannot be rolled back anyway. Compatibility: data format changes are expanding by preference; a breaking change ships an up/down migration pair with a format version; when switching back the loader runs the down migration taken from the generation being left (still on disk) before starting the older one; a failed down leaves data untouched and refuses the switch with a report; a generation that sees a newer format with no way back does not start silently. The self-change gates check a migration pair round-trip (up then down restores the data) and refuse a breaking change without it. Builds on the plugin loader's lifecycle.migrate/hotSwap (ADR-006).

comments.text:
Owner decisions 2026-10-08, continued (supersedes the wizard contents of (5)):
(9) What belongs to the loader: ONLY what lifemodel must not be able to change itself - access to the loader interface, panic, generations (list, boot, maintenance, self-healing), the files/resources/concurrency ceilings of tasks, first start (seed the instance repository, build and start generation 1). Everything else - model endpoint, models per role, request headers (precedent: in ouroboros the owner asked the agent to add custom headers and it did), Telegram, embeddings (a change is lifemodel's own migration), personality, timezone, web search - is lifemodel's OWN settings in its OWN web interface, which it can extend itself. (10) The loader's setup asks only for its password; first acquaintance and settings are led by lifemodel's own interface.
(11) The loader's web interface runs ALWAYS, beside lifemodel, independent of it; changes made there apply immediately (panic at once; a changed key from the next request; network rules even for running tasks; files/resources only for new tasks - Landlock and rlimits cannot change on a running process; the loader may offer to stop a running task).

title: The loader starts lifemodel from the instance's repository on the volume, holds panic and one login
description:
Stage lifemodel-q4x.2, spec stories S1, S2, S6, S7, S8 (feature lifemodel-q4x body).

Criterion: tests through the loader's interfaces with doubles only at process/filesystem boundaries show: first start seeds and starts once, a second start reuses the repository; panic set -> start refused (and normally starts); resume clears; wrong password refused (right one accepted, cookie valid for boot., root, vault. hosts); SIGTERM waits for the child's exit.

title: Tests that run git never touch the repository whose hook started them
description:
A repair the merge of stage lifemodel-q4x.4 waits on (not a finding).

What a person does: commits in this repository with the husky pre-commit hook active (`npm ci` re-enables it through `prepare: husky`; its .husky/pre-commit runs `npx vitest run`).
What happens: git runs the hook with GIT_DIR, GIT_INDEX_FILE (and on a worktree GIT_WORK_TREE/GIT_COMMON_DIR) set; the suite inherits them, and every test that runs git in a temporary directory (loader-seed-git, ci-product-paths, build-image, instance-*, container-image, tool-server-utils, and the loader code they drive) acts on the REAL repository instead. On 2026-10-09 the merge commit of feature/lifemodel-q4x-settings into feature/lifemodel-q4x-instance got a fixture's tree, 14 fixture commits landed on the feature branch, and .git/config was rewritten (bare=true, origin renamed to upstream, core.hooksPath to a deleted temp dir, a test user, gpgsign off, a branch upstream). The owner restored the config by hand; the branch is restored from its reflog (364761a).
What should happen: no test can reach any repository but its own temporary one, wherever the suite is started from (a hook, a shell, CI).

DONE WHEN: (1) the vitest setup removes every GIT_* variable from the environment before any test runs; (2) a guard test runs a git fixture with GIT_DIR/GIT_INDEX_FILE pointing at a sentinel repository and shows the sentinel untouched (and turns red when the scrub is removed); (3) .husky/pre-commit unsets GIT_* before it runs tests; (4) a real `git commit` with the husky hook active in a scratch clone leaves that clone's history and config unchanged apart from the commit itself.
Out: changing which hook a clone uses (`npm run connect` owns that).

title: A disposable launcher bounds and isolates ordinary and Docker test runs
description:
## Problem
Tests started from hooks or shells can alter the real repository, load the owner environment, leave processes and temporary data behind, and overload the machine. Existing fixes on the instance branch do not provide a launch-level boundary.
## Solution
Run local checks and tests through one disposable isolated launcher, also used by CI and hooks. Ordinary tests receive a private source snapshot and disposable HOME/TMP/data with Node 24 and lockfile dependencies, no owner git metadata, secrets, state, or Docker socket. Docker integration tests get a separate disposable daemon, not the owner daemon. Limit CPU, memory, pids, concurrent launches and total runtime. Preserve test exit status and reports. Cleanup from outside the test process on success, failure, timeout and interruption.
## Decisions
Owner 2026-10-09: tests must run locally, but isolated; approved implementation ('Делай'). Workers use shady2k-gateway/glm-5.3-flash. This is a repair of the instance acceptance launch, not a new milestone outcome. Build from main without bundling the unfinished instance product. Never run the existing suite directly on the host. No daemon socket mount or privileged test process. If nested daemon implementation needs a weaker host boundary, stop and report rather than silently grant it.
## Checks
One CLI runs ordinary check/test commands and Docker integration mode. An isolated sentinel scenario proves hostile GIT_* and owner environment/files absent, fixture git cannot mutate the source checkout, and interruption/timeout removes processes and test resources. Static tests cover launch policy and failure paths; real Docker acceptance checks successful test, failing test, cancellation and timeout. Full check runs only through isolation.
## Out
Completing the instance product, generations, task executor, fixing all existing loader assertions, real Telegram or LLM requests, production data.
## DONE WHEN
The local test/check command and hook/CI paths use isolation, preserve meaningful failures and bounded cleanup; hostile owner environment and interrupted test runs cannot modify the real checkout or leave their processes/resources alive. Docker mode uses its own daemon or fails explicitly if unsupported, never falls back to the owner daemon.

Today the news digest is done inside a cognition turn: the schedule news_digest_morning/evening_default (src/plugins/news/index.ts:764-911, handleDailyDigest) wakes cognition, which reads articles and composes the digest while holding the single cognition slot (pendingCognition); only Motor Cortex runs in the background. A message the owner sends meanwhile waits for the digest to end.

Ouroboros (docs/architecture/06-agent-core.md) separates short direct turns (owner chat, wakes) from durable queued tasks with their own lifecycle and stored results.

Proposal: a cognition turn stays short (decide, answer or delegate); long work becomes a task, a generalized Motor Cortex: durable record, recovery after restart (recoverOnRestart exists), result returned as a signal that a short turn delivers. The digest becomes such a task.

Observable criterion: while a digest is being prepared, a message from the owner is answered within the time of an ordinary turn, and the digest still arrives. Disproved if the answer waits for the digest.

Relations: may retire most of lifemodel-aeg (dialogue-1, a message taken into account at every boundary of a proactive turn); a self-change (lifemodel-n6r) also fits as a task.

Left out: choosing the task runner (internal pipeline vs prime-agent), task priorities, cancellation.

Added 2026-10-08 (owner: 'это должны быть задания'): reminders (one-shot and recurring schedule firings) and Motor Cortex results are tasks too. Today a firing is marked done before its signal is processed and a queued signal is lost on a restart or when another turn is busy or the aggregation picks another signal; a completed Motor Cortex result can be lost the same way (pre-existing on main; an acknowledge-after-processing attempt in lifemodel-ctc was rolled back because the core does not know which signals a turn consumed). As tasks they get a durable record and an outcome, so nothing depends on a signal surviving the in-memory queue. Observable criterion added: a reminder due while a turn is busy, or across a restart, is still delivered once.

title: connect-clone.sh still says the product checks wait for npm ci, but the hook now runs the isolated launcher
description:
Once lifemodel-q4x.5.2's launcher wiring lands, `.husky/pre-commit` no longer needs
host `node_modules` for its product checks: it runs lint-staged, then
`node scripts/test-isolated.mjs check` (Node 24 + Docker). But
`scripts/connect-clone.sh` (not owned by q4x.5.2) still prints that the product
checks "are skipped until `npm ci`", and the gate block it appends is unchanged
— correct. The skip message is now stale: the checks are skipped until the
isolated launcher works (node 24 + Docker), not until `npm ci`.

DONE WHEN: scripts/connect-clone.sh's skip message and its connect summary
describe the launcher-based pre-commit (isolated check needs Node.js >= 24 and
Docker, not host node_modules), without weakening the gate blocks or the
.git hooks policy.

Discovered-from: lifemodel-q4x.5.2 (launcher wiring); owned file list of that
task excluded scripts/connect-clone.sh.
